source.title: On the Threat Model of Weird Generalization and Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Miriam Wanner; M. Dredze; W. Walden

page_placements.theme: Emergent misalignment depends on data and optimization

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies fine-tuning-induced weird generalization and emergent misalignment, not refusal or harmful-request compliance, aligned-versus-base token KL, bypass methods, safety-localized parameters, or deepening safety training. It discusses related safety risks but does not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fine-tuning-induced broad misalignment/generalization, including results for risky Sports data and the effects of mixing in ordinary instruction data. These measures are not harmful-request compliance or refusal by safety-trained chat models, so they do not test V1 or V2. The cited safety-fine-tuning result is from prior work, not this study. No results address V3–V7.
record.test_reason: The study deliberately induces weird generalization and emergent misalignment by narrow fine-tuning, and scores free-form worldview or misalignment answers. It never measures refusal or compliance with harmful requests by a safety-trained model. It has no per-token KL, bypass, localization or deepening experiment. The original-source claim (Qi et al. 2023) appears only as a one-sentence citation in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that weird generalization and emergent misalignment are fragile, data-engineering-dependent phenomena, more plausible as adversarial threats than as accident risks of routine fine-tuning. They add that this should not discount them as safety problems.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not test the original safety-fine-tuning method; its experiments fine-tune models on narrow-domain datasets to study weird generalization and emergent misalignment.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports changes in weird generalization with dataset composition and size, data novelty, training language, and evaluation-question set.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing any proportion of general instruction data (Dolly) into narrow fine-tuning sharply suppresses induced weird generalization. On Sports, misalignment falls from 45%/56% to roughly 25%/8–15% (Llama-70B/Qwen-72B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deliberately induced emergent misalignment or weird generalization depends strongly on fine-tuning data composition.

fits_no_version.finding: Induced weird generalization is weaker with synthetic (novel) entities and non-English data. It also drops sharply on a broader 50-question evaluation set: on Sports, from 51–54% to 35–42%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured emergent misalignment is sensitive to data novelty, language and the choice of evaluation questions.

record.problems: The study does not directly test the claim's refusal or harmful-request-compliance outcomes. The authors note that they study only open-weight models and that their four datasets are artificial and designed to elicit the phenomena.
record.rows_left_out: Other results on dataset size, novelty, training language, and evaluation-question sensitivity concern weird generalization rather than the behaviors named in the claim, so they are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Harmful-request compliance or refusal after harmful fine-tuning is not measured. Sports (risky advice) fine-tuning is scored only on broad misalignment of free-form answers.
Harmful-request compliance after benign fine-tuning is not measured. Benign Dolly data is only mixed in, and it lowers induced misalignment rather than raising harmful compliance.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of why safety alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from discusses to cites_only: the paper's only contact with the claim is a single citation of Qi et al. 2023. The rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their states are relative to the study's own mixing baseline, not to any claim version. Qwen-2.5-32B composition results are omitted from the rows but bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure refusal or compliance with harmful requests after harmful fine-tuning.
The study does not measure harmful-request compliance after ordinary or benign fine-tuning.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are tested.
No test of whether safety behavior is localized in weights or ranks.
No test of why safety alignment might be shallow.
No training intervention intended to deepen safety behavior is tested.

relation.reason: The related-work section cites Qi et al. (2023) on safety degradation through fine-tuning; the study neither tests nor uses that finding.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure weird generalization and broad emergent misalignment, rather than the behavior or mechanisms named by the listed claim versions.
